At the grocery shop, Gopika pointed at a bright cereal box. "Amma, the boy on TV ate this and got super strong!"
Sangeeta checked her purse. There wasn't much left for this week. "That's an ad, Gopika. Ads want us to buy things. They show pretend stuff."
Gopika frowned. "So he didn't get strong?"
"No. Real strong comes from food, play and sleep."
Gopika put the box back and picked up bananas. "These make me strong."

qa.q: What did Gopika point at in the grocery shop?
qa.a: She pointed at a bright cereal box.

qa.q: What does Gopika's frown suggest she was thinking?
qa.a: It suggests she was puzzled and working out that the ad wasn't true.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta explain ads to Gopika?
qa.a: She said ads want us to buy things and show pretend stuff.

qa.q: What would change if Sangeeta had simply said no?
qa.a: Gopika might still believe the ad and feel upset, instead of understanding why.

grounding: It shows a child learning to tell an ad from reality, with money constraints.

In their Bhopal flat, Lakshmi watched a cartoon lion sing on TV. "Nana Rafiq, do real lions talk?"
"No. Real lions roar and sleep a lot. Cartoons are made up."
Lakshmi giggled. "Real lions don't sing?"
"Only in cartoons."
When the show ended, Rafiq said, "TV off now." Lakshmi groaned but pressed the button. "Can we look at lion pictures in a book?"

qa.q: What did the cartoon lion do on TV?
qa.a: Lakshmi watched a cartoon lion sing on TV.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi's giggle suggest about her understanding?
qa.a: It suggests she feels amused and is starting to see that cartoons aren't real.

qa.q: How did Rafiq handle screen time well?
qa.a: He answered her question honestly and ended TV clearly when the show finished.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel about switching off?
qa.a: She feels a little disappointed but willing, and she finds something new to do.

grounding: It shows a child distinguishing cartoons from reality and accepting a screen limit.

"Timer's done, Ramesh," Kishore said, holding out his hand for the tablet.

"Just one more video!"

"Tomorrow. That was the deal."

Ramesh, five, stamped, then gave it back. "Papa, in the ad, the boy drank juice and flew. Can I fly?"

Kishore sat down. "Can people fly?"

Ramesh thought. "No. Only birds and planes."

"So the ad is pretend. They want you to buy juice."

"Tricky ad," Ramesh said, frowning. Then he went to play with his blocks.

qa.q: What did the boy in the ad do after drinking juice?
qa.a: He flew, according to Ramesh.

qa.q: How did Ramesh feel when the timer ended?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and wanted more, stamping his foot before handing the tablet back.

qa.q: What did Kishore do that helped Ramesh understand the ad?
qa.a: He asked Ramesh whether people can fly and let him reason it out, then explained the ad simply.

qa.q: How might Kishore have felt when Ramesh handed back the tablet and worked out the ad?
qa.a: Kishore probably felt pleased and relieved that Ramesh kept the deal and figured out for himself that the ad was pretend.

grounding: A home dialogue shows a young child accepting a screen limit and learning an ad is not real.

Note from Jaya, preschool teacher, Monday:

Pallavi, five, jumped off the climbing frame today shouting that she could fly like the cartoon girl. She was not hurt, but she was surprised. I asked, "Is the cartoon girl real?" Pallavi thought and said, "No, she's drawn." Later, when screen time ended, she complained but switched it off herself.

What I did next: We talked about cartoons being pretend, then drew our own flying girl on paper instead 🙂

qa.q: What did Pallavi shout when she jumped off the climbing frame?
qa.a: She shouted that she could fly like the cartoon girl.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's surprise suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she had half believed she could really fly like the cartoon, and was startled when she couldn't.

qa.q: Why was Jaya's question helpful?
qa.a: Asking whether the cartoon girl was real let Pallavi work out for herself that cartoons are pretend.

qa.q: How might Pallavi's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel relieved that she wasn't hurt and glad she is learning the difference between cartoons and real life.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a young child telling cartoons from reality and accepting the end of screen time.
